title: Eleven Rigs Asleep
passages:
Miko rode the running board with her boots hooked over the frame and the wind packing dust down her collar. She had no name. Brill had rubbed her inked name off the storeroom steel, and her badge—C9-047—sat on a dead-name manifest clipped to Culvert Nine's board. She was cargo now, or something closer to it: a body without a plate, riding north on a rig that belonged to a man who kept names in a book.

Dray slowed the rig at the edge of Marrow Cut. The yard's door plate stood in the dirt—a slab of steel bolted to two posts, stamped with the yard's number and a line of rules Miko couldn't read from the running board. Dray cut the engine. The rig settled. The only sound was the tick of cooling metal and the wind down the spur.

"Out," Dray said.

Miko dropped to the ground. Her knees took the weight. Dray didn't offer a hand. He walked her to a scale bolted beside the door plate: a cast-iron platform with a dial face and a sliding weight. He gestured at it with his chin.

"Step on."

"I'm not freight," Miko said.

"Then say your name," Dray said.

Miko opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She had coast tickets under three bought names, but none of them were hers anymore. She had burned the last two. She had nothing.

"Scale doesn't care," Dray said. "Step on."

She stepped on. The dial spun and stopped at a number—one-twenty-seven, maybe, though she wasn't looking at the numbers so much as the man writing them down in a ledger bolted to the scale housing. Dray didn't introduce himself as the writer. He just wrote.

"One-twenty-seven," Dray said. "Short rate. You draw water at the short rate until you're read out at the plate. Second bell, you're either on a plate or on the shelf with the sleepers. Understand?"

Miko looked past him at the shed. The roll door was climbing, slow and groaning, and behind it rose eleven dark shapes. Off-board rigs. Transponders pulled. No board to answer to. They sat in the dark. They did not move.

"And if I don't want either?" Miko asked.

Dray looked at her, expressionless. "Then you stay on the scale until someone names you. The yard doesn't run on wants."

Miko shifted her weight. The iron was cold through her boots. "What happens to the sleepers?"

"They sleep until a plate dies," Dray said. "Then they go on the pile. You want to be a pile?"

"No."

"Then find a name before the second bell." He pointed at the shed. The door kept climbing. Eleven rigs. Forty riders, he had said. Forty plates wired shut to sternums. And one name missing from her own chest.

Miko spat into the dirt. "I had a name once. Culvert Nine's station loader. Badge C9-047."

"Then you should have kept it," Dray said. He turned and walked toward the shed, his boots heavy on the gravel. "Second bell rings when that door hits the top."

Miko stood on the scale. The dial still read one-twenty-seven. Ahead, the eleventh dark shape rose into the light, silent and blank, waiting for someone to say its name.
